Family Health

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: types, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, often shortened to NHL, is a group of cancers arising from lymphocytes, cells that normally help the body defend itself. Some forms grow slowly; others can progress quickly. Understanding the exact diagnosis is essential because two people described as having lymphoma may need very different treatment and follow-up.

What lymphoma means

Lymphoma develops when lymphocytes become abnormal and multiply in an uncontrolled way. It can involve lymph nodes, but it is not simply another name for every cancer found in a lymph node. A cancer that starts in another organ and spreads to nearby nodes remains classified according to its original type.

The broad distinction between Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is made through specialist examination of tissue and other laboratory findings. Characteristic Reed–Sternberg cells are associated with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, but diagnosis requires more than recognizing a large abnormal cell. Some other conditions can have look-alike cells.

NHL is more common than Hodgkin lymphoma overall. Neither label, by itself, provides enough information to choose treatment. Ask for the complete pathology name and an explanation of what it means.

The lymphatic system and the cells involved

The lymphatic system supports immune defence and returns fluid from tissues to the bloodstream. Its network includes vessels and lymph nodes, as well as lymphatic tissue in several organs.

Important sites include the spleen, bone marrow, thymus, tonsils and adenoids. Lymphatic tissue is also present in places such as the digestive tract and skin. Lymphoma can therefore begin outside a readily felt lymph node; this is called an extranodal site.

B cells help defend against infection by making antibodies. T cells have several roles, including coordinating immune activity and destroying infected or abnormal cells. Natural killer cells, or NK cells, also help recognize and attack certain abnormal cells.

Different lymphomas arise from different points in the development of these cells. The cell of origin, its appearance and laboratory markers help explain why the diseases behave differently and why a medicine used for one subtype may not suit another.

The main types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

B-cell lymphomas account for most NHL. The American Cancer Society describes approximately 85% of US cases as B-cell types; T-cell types make up less than 15%. These are broad US figures, and the distribution varies by population. NK-cell-associated forms are uncommon.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, or DLBCL, is a common fast-growing subtype. Follicular lymphoma is another common B-cell type and is usually slower-growing. ACS estimates describe roughly one in three US lymphomas as DLBCL and one in five as follicular lymphoma; these figures are not a prediction of an individual’s diagnosis.

Other B-cell diagnoses include Burkitt lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and small lymphocytic lymphoma. The names identify different diseases rather than interchangeable descriptions of a single cancer.

The words indolent and aggressive describe a usual pattern of growth. Indolent disease often grows slowly, while aggressive disease tends to progress faster. Adult NHL includes both groups. “Aggressive” does not automatically mean that treatment cannot work, and “indolent” does not mean that follow-up is unnecessary.

How childhood lymphoma differs

The mix of NHL diagnoses in children and adolescents differs from that in older adults. Important pediatric types include Burkitt lymphoma, lymphoblastic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and anaplastic large cell lymphoma.

Many childhood NHL types grow quickly. A child with a suspected or confirmed diagnosis needs a pediatric cancer team; adult watch-and-wait advice should not be applied at home to a child with an enlarging lump.

Children’s treatment plans take the subtype, disease distribution and other findings into account. Longer-term follow-up also considers growth, development and possible later effects of treatment. Families should ask the team to explain the name of the disease and the purpose of each planned test.

Symptoms and the meaning of B symptoms

Possible symptoms include enlarged lymph nodes, unusual fatigue, unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Some people also have itching, a rash or skin lumps. These findings have many possible causes and are not a diagnosis on their own.

Symptoms can reflect where the lymphoma is located. Abdominal disease may cause pain, swelling, reduced appetite or a feeling of fullness. Disease in the chest can be associated with cough, chest discomfort or difficulty breathing.

Clinicians use the term B symptoms for particular systemic symptoms: unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and substantial unexplained weight loss, conventionally more than 10% of body weight over six months. Not every person has all of them. They help describe the illness but do not establish its subtype or stage by themselves.

Arrange assessment for persistent or unexplained symptoms. An infection is a common reason for enlarged lymph nodes, but a lump that persists or grows needs review. Severe breathing difficulty, especially with new face or neck swelling, warrants urgent help.

Why lymphoma develops

Changes in the DNA of a lymphocyte can disrupt the normal controls on its growth and survival. These changes can involve individual genes, missing genetic material or rearrangements in chromosomes. A translocation, for example, moves genetic material into a different arrangement.

Finding a genetic change in cancer cells does not automatically mean it was inherited from a parent. Many relevant changes arise during a person’s life. A family history may affect risk, but it cannot explain every case or predict that another relative will become ill.

Researchers have identified several associations with NHL, but an individual’s cancer often has no single identifiable cause. Older age increases the opportunity for cellular changes to accumulate, yet some subtypes occur in young adults and children.

A diagnosis is not evidence that someone failed to look after their health. It is possible to have several risk factors and never develop lymphoma, or to develop it without a recognized risk factor.

Risk factors: age, family history and exposures

Overall, NHL is more common in older adults, particularly from the sixties onwards, and is more common in men than women. Individual subtypes can follow a different pattern. Having a parent, sibling or child with NHL can also raise risk without making the disease inevitable.

Rates differ between populations and geographical areas. US statistics report a higher overall incidence among White people than among Black or Asian American people. This does not identify the cause of a particular person’s illness or provide reassurance that someone in another group cannot be affected.

Certain chemical exposures, including some herbicides and insecticides, have been investigated as possible risk factors. Evidence varies by exposure and subtype. Significant radiation exposure and some previous cancer treatments are also relevant parts of a medical history.

Some studies suggest an association with excess body weight, but this is not a simple cause-and-effect rule for every lymphoma. Discuss relevant exposures and previous treatment with the clinician; an online checklist cannot calculate a personal diagnosis.

Immune conditions, infections and breast implants

A weakened immune system can increase the risk of some lymphomas. Examples include HIV infection and immune-suppressing treatment after an organ transplant. Autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, Sjögren disease and celiac disease are also associated with certain lymphoma types, through pathways that are not identical to simple immune deficiency.

Some infections have more specific associations. Epstein–Barr virus is linked with several lymphoma subtypes. Hepatitis C can be relevant to certain B-cell lymphomas. Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that can infect the stomach, is associated with gastric MALT lymphoma through chronic immune stimulation; it should not be described as the same kind of DNA-transforming virus as EBV.

Chlamydophila psittaci has been associated with MALT lymphoma around the eye in some settings. These links do not mean that most people with the infection will develop lymphoma. Tests and infection treatment should follow the individual clinical assessment.

Breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma, or BIA-ALCL, is a rare T-cell lymphoma usually found in fluid or scar tissue around an implant. It is distinct from the usual forms of breast cancer. Risk is higher with textured than with smooth implants.

Persistent swelling, a new lump or pain around an implant should be assessed, even years after placement. The FDA does not recommend routine removal solely because of this concern in people without symptoms. A clinician can discuss the individual device, findings and next steps.

Examination and initial tests

A clinician asks about symptoms, their duration, medical history and possible infections, and examines the areas of concern. The examination may assess lymph nodes and look for enlargement of the liver or spleen.

Blood tests can check blood-cell counts, organ function and markers such as LDH. They may also investigate infections or help prepare for treatment. A normal routine blood result does not necessarily exclude lymphoma, and an abnormal result does not establish its subtype.

Urine testing may be appropriate when another suspected condition or infection needs investigation, but it is not a definitive lymphoma test. The purpose of each test should be clear: finding an explanation for symptoms, establishing the diagnosis, assessing extent or planning care.

Biopsy, imaging and staging

Diagnosis generally requires examination of affected tissue. A biopsy may remove a whole lymph node, part of one, or an appropriate sample from another site. Laboratory assessment considers cell appearance and features such as proteins and genetic changes; enough tissue is needed to classify the disease accurately.

Imaging may include CT or PET/CT, with ultrasound, MRI or a chest X-ray used for particular questions. Not every person needs every scan. A PET scan shows patterns of tracer uptake but is not a substitute for the tissue diagnosis.

A bone marrow sample may be useful in selected cases. Whether it is needed depends on the subtype, blood results, imaging and the information the team requires. A conventional bone scan is a different examination and is not a routine staging requirement for all NHL.

Staging describes where lymphoma is present in the body. It is considered alongside subtype, symptoms and other prognostic findings. Blood tests contribute information but cannot, alone, determine the full extent of the disease.

Ask when the complete pathology and staging results will be available. Sometimes an initial description changes after specialist review or additional laboratory testing. That refinement can materially affect the proposed treatment.

Why treatment may start now: or after monitoring

Treatment decisions depend on the exact lymphoma, its behaviour and extent, symptoms, general health, previous treatment and the person’s priorities. Age is one consideration, not the only deciding factor.

For some slow-growing lymphomas that are not causing problems, active monitoring can be appropriate. It involves planned appointments and instructions about changes to report. It is not an instruction to ignore symptoms until they become severe.

More aggressive disease commonly needs prompt treatment. Some treatment plans aim for cure; others aim for long-term control or relief of symptoms. The team should explain the goal and how response will be assessed.

Regulatory approval, availability and the evidence for a medicine vary by subtype, treatment setting and country. An off-label use may sometimes be considered by a specialist, but a general list of drugs is not proof that each is approved or appropriate for every NHL.

Chemotherapy and corticosteroids

Chemotherapy can be given intravenously or by mouth, often using a combination selected for the lymphoma. Treatment is commonly arranged in cycles, allowing periods for recovery between administrations.

Alkylating agents used in lymphoma care include cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, bendamustine and ifosfamide. Prednisone and dexamethasone are corticosteroids that can be components of lymphoma regimens.

Fludarabine, pentostatin and cladribine are purine analogues, not platinum drugs. Cisplatin, carboplatin and oxaliplatin belong to the platinum group.

Other examples include the antimetabolites cytarabine, gemcitabine, methotrexate and pralatrexate; the anthracycline doxorubicin; and medicines such as vincristine, mitoxantrone, etoposide and bleomycin. These names identify options across different settings, not a list that a patient should receive together.

Ask for the names and purpose of the actual regimen, its schedule, expected side effects and a contact number for urgent concerns. Report fever or sudden illness according to the treatment team’s instructions rather than waiting for the next routine appointment.

Radiotherapy and stem cell transplantation

Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at a planned area to treat lymphoma cells. It may be used on its own for selected localized disease, alongside other treatments, or to relieve symptoms. Its role depends on the subtype and the purpose of treatment.

A stem cell transplant can allow selected patients to receive intensive treatment that also damages blood-forming cells. An infusion of stem cells then helps restore blood production. This is a major treatment with substantial monitoring and recovery needs.

An autologous transplant uses the person’s own cells, collected and stored beforehand. An allogeneic transplant uses cells from a suitable donor. The benefits and risks differ, and transplantation is not required for everyone with lymphoma.

Before intensive treatment, ask about infection precautions, recovery, fertility and longer-term effects. These conversations should be tailored to the planned therapy and, where relevant, involve an age-appropriate pediatric team.

Antibody treatments and immunotherapy

Monoclonal antibodies recognize particular targets on cells. Examples include rituximab and obinutuzumab, which target CD20, and tafasitamab, which targets CD19. Ofatumumab is another anti-CD20 antibody, although use and availability depend on the setting.

Some antibodies carry an additional treatment. Brentuximab vedotin targets CD30 and polatuzumab vedotin targets CD79b; each carries a cell-killing medicine. Ibritumomab tiuxetan is an example of a radiolabelled antibody approach. Alemtuzumab targets CD52.

These markers are not exclusive labels found on every cancer of one cell type. Selection depends on the diagnosis and treatment evidence, not merely recognizing “B cell” or “T cell” in a name.

Immune-modifying medicines include lenalidomide and, in certain settings, thalidomide. Their use requires specialist oversight, including strict pregnancy-prevention measures because of serious fetal harm. An older drug name in an article should never be treated as a self-treatment option.

Newer immune treatments also include bispecific antibodies that bring immune cells and lymphoma cells together. Infusion reactions, infections and other serious effects require the team’s prevention and monitoring plan.

What CAR T-cell therapy involves

CAR stands for chimeric antigen receptor. In CAR T-cell therapy, T cells collected from the patient are modified in a laboratory so they can recognize a particular target on cancer cells. The cells are expanded and returned to the patient as a treatment.

This approach is used for defined lymphoma situations, not for every newly diagnosed patient. Suitability depends on the subtype, previous response, available products and the person’s health.

CAR T-cell therapy can cause serious reactions, including cytokine release syndrome and neurological problems. It is delivered through teams trained to monitor and treat those complications. Ask what monitoring, caregiver support and proximity to the treatment centre will be required.

Other targeted medicines and changing approvals

Targeted medicines act on pathways that help cancer cells survive or grow. They can be used in several treatment settings; they are not all reserved for a point when every chemotherapy option has failed.

Examples of classes include proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib, histone deacetylase inhibitors such as belinostat, and Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as ibrutinib and acalabrutinib. Their uses differ by diagnosis.

PI3K inhibitors include idelalisib and duvelisib. Some lymphoma indications for these medicines have been withdrawn in the United States, so an older list can give a misleading impression of current options. Similarly, the former US mantle-cell and marginal-zone lymphoma indications for ibrutinib were withdrawn, while other uses remain.

A targeted medicine can still cause serious adverse effects or interact with other medicines. Ask why the proposed treatment fits your particular disease and which current guidance supports it. Do not change prescribed therapy solely because another person’s lymphoma was treated differently.

Can non-Hodgkin lymphoma be prevented?

There is no way to guarantee prevention of NHL. Age, family history and many of the cellular changes involved cannot be controlled. General advice should not imply that a person could certainly have avoided the diagnosis.

Reducing exposure to HIV and hepatitis C has important health benefits. Safer-sex practices, sterile injection equipment and appropriate testing or prevention services can help reduce infection risks. People already living with an infection should receive appropriate care rather than blame.

Physical activity, balanced eating and support for a healthy weight benefit overall health. A pattern including fruit, vegetables and whole grains, with fewer sugary drinks and highly processed foods, can be helpful, but it is not a proven guarantee against lymphoma.

If an infection or immune condition is already diagnosed, follow its treatment plan. Do not stop an immune-suppressing medicine on your own because of a risk-factor list; the benefits and risks require individual assessment.

Understanding prognosis and follow-up

Outlook depends on the subtype, extent of disease, general health, age and response to treatment. A statistic for all NHL combines very different illnesses and cannot tell an individual what will happen.

Some slow-growing lymphomas can be managed over a long period, sometimes with intervals when treatment is not needed. Some aggressive lymphomas can be cured. The words fast-growing and incurable are not interchangeable.

An advanced stage also does not automatically rule out treatment with curative intent. The meaning of stage in lymphoma differs from assumptions people may have about other cancers. Ask the team what the treatment goal is for the exact diagnosis.

Follow-up may assess remission, recurrence and treatment effects. Supportive or palliative care can also help with symptoms and quality of life alongside cancer treatment; it is not limited to the final days of life.

You do not need both a known risk factor and a symptom before seeking advice. Persistent unexplained symptoms deserve assessment in their own right, while a confirmed diagnosis calls for a plan specific to that lymphoma.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

National Cancer Institute information distinguishes slow-growing and aggressive lymphomas and describes diagnosis, staging and treatment as subtype-specific processes. A broad lymphoma label is not enough to select a treatment.

American Cancer Society guidance explains the roles of chemotherapy, immune treatment and targeted medicines. Current regulatory information also matters because a medicine’s approved uses can change.

How BeMama can help

BeMama offers general health education for families preparing for a medical conversation. It cannot classify lymphoma, interpret a biopsy or recommend a cancer regimen. Keep the full diagnosis and the treatment team’s contact details with your appointment notes.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for persistent unexplained swelling or systemic symptoms. Severe breathing difficulty or rapidly developing face or neck swelling needs urgent help. During cancer treatment, follow the team’s urgent-contact instructions for fever or sudden illness.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • NHL includes many diseases; the complete pathology diagnosis matters.
  • Adults can have slow-growing or aggressive disease, and childhood patterns differ.
  • Symptoms and blood tests alone cannot establish the diagnosis or full stage.
  • Active monitoring is appropriate only for selected cases with a clinical follow-up plan.
  • Drug classes, approvals and treatment goals differ by subtype and can change over time.
  • Advanced stage does not automatically mean that curative treatment is impossible.

Frequently asked questions

Does a swollen lymph node mean lymphoma?

No. Infection and other conditions can enlarge lymph nodes. Persistent or growing swelling should be assessed, particularly when accompanied by unexplained systemic symptoms.

Is all adult NHL fast-growing?

No. Adult NHL includes indolent and aggressive forms. The specific subtype is more informative than the umbrella name.

Can a routine blood test rule it out?

No. Blood tests contribute useful information, but normal results do not necessarily exclude lymphoma. Tissue examination is generally needed to establish the diagnosis.

Why might the team recommend monitoring instead of immediate treatment?

Some slow-growing lymphomas can be monitored safely when they are not causing problems. This requires a planned clinical schedule and clear instructions about changes to report.

Are all medicines in a lymphoma drug list suitable for me?

No. Each medicine has particular indications, combinations, risks and availability. Some older approvals have changed or been withdrawn.

Is CAR T-cell therapy the same as a stem cell transplant?

No. CAR T-cell therapy modifies immune cells to recognize a cancer target. A stem cell transplant restores blood-forming cells after intensive treatment; the purposes and procedures differ.

Does stage IV always mean treatment cannot cure the lymphoma?

No. Some lymphomas remain potentially curable at an advanced stage. The treating team can explain what stage means for the particular subtype and circumstances.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
